name: False African Violet
summary: Streptocarpus saxorum is a separate accepted species sometimes called false African violet or Cape primrose. NC State Extension describes its small trailing habit, shade-grown container use, shallow roots, and seed, division or stem-cutting propagation.

identity.short: Accepted species distinct from the African violet
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Streptocarpus saxorum from southeast Kenya to Tanzania. NC State uses false African violet, Cape primrose and Cape violet; the similar common name does not make this the Streptocarpus ionanthus African violet identity.

growth.short: Small mounding perennial with spring–summer flowers
growth.guidance: NC State reports up to about 8 inches tall and 12 inches wide, with soft green leaves and small tubular flowers whose white throats open into lilac-to-violet lobes. Bloom is usually in spring and summer and may continue into winter. These dimensions and characteristics refer to S. saxorum, not to African violet cultivars or the broader Streptocarpus genus.

cultivation.short: Warm, sheltered shade and drained, humus-rich medium
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension recommends light shade, a warm sheltered location, and well-drained humus-rich soil or a loam-based container mix. It advises allowing the mix to dry between watering because roots are shallow; this does not establish hydroponic suitability.

maintenance.short: Remove spent growth and avoid waterlogging
maintenance.guidance: NC State recommends removing dead or unhealthy flowers and foliage and protecting the plant from drying winds. Stem cuttings are a documented alternative to seed, while division is listed for larger established plants.

problems.short: Overwatering and strong midday sun can damage the plant
problems.guidance: NC State notes root rot from overwatering, fungal disease risk, mealybugs and caterpillars, and leaf scorch from direct midday sunlight. It recommends good air circulation to reduce fungal problems.

propagation.short: Seed, division and stem cuttings are documented
propagation.guidance: NC State Extension says plants may be grown from seed in early spring and also lists division and stem cuttings. The source does not give depth, temperature, germination duration or seedling-transplant criteria; see the linked Seed Profile for those explicit unknowns.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Container-soil guidance does not establish hydroponic compatibility.

evidence.note: NC State describes this species as small, mounding and trailing.
